extracted.intended_audience: senior undergraduate mathematics students (preparing a senior comprehensive paper) and authors of mathematical papers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for the style, formatting, citation, theorem/proof presentation, and numbering conventions for senior comprehensive papers and mathematical articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended references on mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: References recommended for information on the writing of mathematical papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists three pamphlets to consult: 'Writing Mathematics Well' by Leonard Gillman; 'How to Write Mathematics' by Paul Halmos; 'A Primer of Mathematical Writing' by Steven G. Krantz. (Copies available in the library.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Form for the bibliography (ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliography items should be listed in alphabetical order based on the author's last name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given to illustrate ordering and formats for entries. Ensure last-name alphabetical order when assembling the bibliography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form for the bibliography (entry formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific formatting examples for different kinds of bibliography entries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: journal article entry format ([1] R. P. Boas, "Can We Make Mathematics Intelligible?", Amer. Math. Monthly 88(1981), 727-731.); article from a book ([2] Paul R. Halmos, "How to Write Mathematics", in Selecta, Expository Writing, Springer, 1983, 157-186.); and a book ([3] John von Neumann and Oskar Morgenstern, Theory of Games and Economic Behavior, Princeton University Press, 1947.). Follow these models for punctuation, order of fields, and abbreviation style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation style (in-text references)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to cite references within the text using bracketed bibliography numbers and page references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '...order of the local truncation error [5,p.56]' where [5] is the reference number as listed in your bibliography. Use the bracketed-number style and include page numbers when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not begin a sentence with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with mathematical symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example anti-pattern: 'G is an abelian group.' Preferred: 'The group G is abelian.' Rephrase sentences so they begin with words rather than standalone symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'we' rather than 'I' when describing your plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the first-person plural ('we') instead of the singular ('I') in expository or planning remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a stylistic convention in mathematical writing to present collective reasoning or the paper's plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice over passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use active constructions in preference to passive ones for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write statements that make the actor explicit where appropriate (e.g., 'We prove...' rather than 'It is proved that...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples liberally
rubrics_metrics.description: Include examples frequently to illustrate definitions, theorems, and arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide explicitly advises liberal use of examples to aid reader understanding; follow this principle throughout the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: If...then usage: include 'then' after 'if' when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When beginning a sentence with 'if', do not forget to include the corresponding 'then' when it clarifies the logical structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaving out the 'then' can confuse the reader. Use 'If ... then ...' to make conditional statements clear when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize terms being defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for terms at the point where they are defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide emphasizes italicizing defined terms (example referenced in item 6). This helps signal definitions to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use standard notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt conventional mathematical notation for common objects (functions, variables, standard sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use f for a function, x for a variable, n for a natural number. Avoid idiosyncratic symbols where standard choices exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place long or complicated expressions on their own line
rubrics_metrics.description: If an expression is long or complicated, display it on a separate line rather than inline with text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves readability; the guide explicitly instructs to put long/complicated expressions on a line by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing between symbols and adjacent text
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave a double space between symbols and adjacent text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast 'Let z be a complex number' with a spacing variant; the instruction indicates using extra spacing to separate symbols from surrounding words for clarity. (The document shows examples illustrating correct vs incorrect spacing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid logical-quantifier symbols in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the symbolic forms 'for all' (∀) or 'there exists' (∃) in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out quantifiers in words rather than using the symbols when writing prose: e.g., write 'for all' or 'there exists' instead of the symbolic notation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem/proof presentation (set-off and indentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems and their proofs should be set off from surrounding expository material; proofs should be block-indented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the theorem statement clearly labeled (e.g., '6.5 Theorem: ...') then present the proof as an indented block. The guide includes an example excerpt demonstrating this style.

rubrics_metrics.name: End-of-proof marker (QED / box) optional
rubrics_metrics.description: A visible end-of-proof marker is standard but choice of symbol is flexible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: 'Note that we did not use a cute symbol to mark the end of the proof. You may use the symbol of your choice; QED or a box are standard choices.' Use a consistent end-of-proof marker (QED, □, or similar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbering system for chapters and numbered items
rubrics_metrics.description: Each chapter should be numbered; numbered items within a chapter should use chapter_number.ordinal (e.g., 3.1, 3.2, ...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example structure: Chapter 3 The Derivative; 3.1 Definition: ...; 3.2 Example: ...; 3.4 Lemma: ...; 3.5 Theorem: ...; etc. Use this hierarchical numbering for definitions, examples, lemmas, theorems, corollaries, and proofs in senior comprehensive papers.
